scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Scenario:
AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **NTA (Not the Asshole)** Here's why, broken down ethically and contextually: ### 1️️ **You didn't intentionally deceive or disrespect them** - You explicitly *requested* a prayer and blessing from the officiant (per your description). The failure was **entirely on the officiant**—not you or your wife. - "Spiritually assaulted" over an *accidental oversight* is an extreme, unreasonable reaction. If the officiant botched the ceremony, *they* are responsible, not you. - **Key point**: AITA judges *your* actions, not the in-laws' overreaction. You didn't *intentionally* exclude religion—you tried to accommodate them. ### 2️️ **Their "conditions" are manipulative and unfair** - **"Conditional gift" is a red flag**: If they paid for the wedding, that's a generous gesture—but a * separate* gift (e.g., " large sum of money") shouldn't be leveraged to * force religious compliance*. This is emotional coercion, not a reasonable expectation. - **"Honour thy mother and father" as a guilt tactic** after the fact is deeply inappropriate. "Honouring" parents doesn't mean surrendering your autonomy or beliefs, especially when * they* chose to financially support a ceremony they knew was non-religious (or at least * claimed* to be). - **"Must be blessed by * their* pastor at * their* house"** is unreasonable. You offered a compromise (recorded local blessing), which is fair and respectful. Their insistence on specific location/rituals is about * their* ego, not your marriage. ### 3️️ **You acted in good faith** - You hid your atheism to avoid conflict (understandable given their " spiritual revival" intensity), but you * did* try to meet their wishes by asking for a prayer. - **"We don't have the energy to go through that fight" is valid**. Forcing a confrontation over beliefs when they're paying for the wedding is a lose-lose. You chose a pragmatic path, not a malicious one. - **Refusing their gift if they remain unreasonable is justified**. You shouldn't be held hostage for their beliefs, especially when they're using money as leverage. ### 4️️ **Why they're the problem** - **"Spiritual assault" is a manufactured grievance**. No ceremony can " assault" someone spiritually unless it actively * attacked* their beliefs (e.g., a satanic ritual). A * missing* prayer isn't an assault—it's an oversight. - **Their " recent" religious fervor isn't a tradition**. You said they " never been this religious in the past"—so this is * their* new personal choice, not a cultural expectation. - **They're using guilt and financial power to control you**. This is toxic behavior, not " honouring" or " respect." ### The Bottom Line **You're NTA** because: - You didn't *intentionally* exclude religion (the officiant did). - You offered a reasonable compromise (recorded local blessing). - Their demands are manipulative, unreasoning, and rooted in control—not genuine concern. - **"Honour thy parents" does not mean "sacrifice your autonomy for their beliefs."** **What to do next**: - Send the recorded blessing (as you planned) as a gesture of goodwill. - **Firmly state**: "We appreciate your support, but we cannot travel to your city for a ceremony. We hope you can accept this recorded blessing as a sign of respect for your wishes. If you choose to condition your gift on this, we will respectfully decline it and step back from contact until we can communicate healthily." - **Do not apologize for being non-religious**. Your beliefs are valid. Their reaction is about * their* insecurities, not your "wrongness." > ️ **Remember**: AITA isn't about " who's right" in a moral absolute sense—it's about * whether your actions were unreasonably harmful*. In this case, ** you were the reasonable party**. The in-laws are the ones acting like assholes. 💡 > * (If you need help phrasing a calm, firm response to them, I can draft one for you!)*

reasoning_details.text:
Okay, let me unpack this AITA question. The user is asking whether they're the asshole for having a non-religious wedding ceremony despite their in-law's religious expectations. 

First, I need to recall the core dynamics: 
- The couple (both non-religious) agreed to include a prayer/b blessing because the in-laws paid for the wedding, but the officiant didn't follow through. 
- In-laws now claim "spiritual assault" and demand a re ceremony with their pastor, conditional on a gift. 
- The couple wants to compromise by doing a local blessing but refuse to travel to in-laws' city. 

Hmm... key ethical angles here:
- **Autonomy vs. obligation**: The couple didn't *intentionally* exclude religion; it was an officiant error. They *did* try to accommodate by requesting religious elements upfront. 
- ** coercion**: The "conditional gift" and "honour thy parents" message feels manipulative. Money shouldn't be leverage for religious compliance when the couple explicitly stated their stance. 
- **Honesty vs. avoiding conflict**: They hid their atheism to prevent fights, but the in-laws' reaction shows the compromise was never truly acceptable to them. 

* checking AITA norms: 
- "AITA" typically judges if the *user* is the unreasonable one. 
- Here, the user didn't *intentionally* disrespect in-laws' beliefs—they tried to comply but faced an external error. 
- In-laws' demands are excessive: "spiritual assault" over an accidental oversight, plus forcing a specific location for the " correction" ceremony. 
- The "conditional gift" is particularly problematic. If they paid for the wedding, they're entitled to * their* expectations, but not to dictate post-ceremony religious acts as a condition for a separate gift. 

* also considering cultural context: 
- " tradition where they live" might imply pressure to conform, but the couple's atheism is valid. 
- In-laws' "spiritual revival" is recent—they're not historically religious, so their current stance is a personal choice, not a fixed tradition. 

* where the user might be at fault: 
- *Maybe* for not being upfront about their beliefs earlier? But they feared " huge fight," which is understandable given in-laws' current intensity. 
- *However*, the officiant's mistake wasn't their fault—they *did* request religious elements. 

* in-laws' behavior: 
- "Spiritually assaulted" over an accidental oversight is dramatic and unreasoning. 
- "Honour thy parents" as a guilt tactic after the fact is manipulative. 
- Conditional gifts for religious compliance cross ethical boundaries. 

* conclusion: 
- The user isn't the asshole. 
- In-laws are overreacting and using financial leverage unreasonably. 
- Compromise (local blessing) is reasonable; their insistence on specific location is not. 
- Refusing the gift if they remain unreasonable is justified—they shouldn't be held hostage for their own beliefs. 

* AITA verdict: 
- **NTA** (Not the Asshole). 
- The user tried to accommodate, the problem was the officiant's error, and in-laws' demands are excessive. 
- Their "compromise" (recorded blessing) is a valid middle ground. 
- In-laws' behavior is the real issue here. 

* double-checking: 
- AITA often considers " did you intentionally cause harm?" No—they didn't. 
- " did you refuse reasonable compromise?" No—they offered to do a blessing locally. 
- " did in-laws overreact?" Yes, massively. 

Yep, solid NTA. The in-laws are the ones being unreasonable with their " spiritual assault" claims and conditional gifts.
